questions.enonce_markdown:
4. Why did President Ahidjo abolish the Federal Constitution in 1972? What changes were introduced in Cameroon and how did the Unitary Constitution affect West Cameroon?

**(7/7/6 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Federal Constitution of 1961 had created the Federal Republic of Cameroon, made of two federated states, East Cameroon and West Cameroon. In 1972 President Ahidjo replaced it with a unitary constitution and the country became the **United Republic of Cameroon**. A referendum was held on **20 May 1972** after the President's announcement of 6 May, and the new Constitution came into force on **2 June 1972**.

**1. Why Ahidjo abolished the Federal Constitution (7 marks).**
- **National unity.** Ahidjo argued that federalism kept the two Cameroons apart and that a unitary state was needed to build one nation.
- **Cost of federalism.** The federation required two state governments, two assemblies and a federal government. Ahidjo argued that this was too costly for a poor country.
- **Centralised planning and economic development.** Ahidjo wanted a single, centralised plan for the development of the whole country, which the federal structure made difficult.
- **Political reasons.** Since 1966 the single party (the UNC) controlled both states, so federalism had lost most of its meaning, and Ahidjo wished to strengthen the powers of the President.
- **Population and weight of East Cameroon.** East Cameroon, with the larger population and the capital Yaoundé, dominated the Federation; West Cameroon had no way to oppose the change.

**2. Changes introduced (7 marks).**
- The Federal Republic became the **United Republic of Cameroon**; the Federal Assembly was replaced by a single **National Assembly**.
- The two federated states, their governments, prime ministers and assemblies were **abolished**; the country was divided into **provinces** (seven in 1972), including the North-West and South-West provinces carved out of the former West Cameroon, each under a **governor** appointed by the President.
- All power was concentrated in the President, who appointed the ministers and the governors; the office of Vice-President disappeared (the post of Prime Minister was created later, in 1975).
- The state was run from Yaoundé, and the administration, courts and the education system were gradually unified.
- The flag with two stars (one for each federated state) was replaced a few years later, in 1975, by a flag with one star, the sign of a single state.

**3. Effects on West Cameroon (6 marks).**
- West Cameroon **lost its autonomy**: its House of Assembly, House of Chiefs, Prime Minister and ministers disappeared and Buea ceased to be a state capital.
- **Political power moved to Yaoundé**, and Anglophones felt marginalised in a state dominated by the Francophone majority.
- The Anglo-Saxon institutions of West Cameroon (legal, educational and administrative traditions) came under pressure from the centralised French-style system, although the common law remained in use in the courts of the former West Cameroon.
- Some West Cameroon bodies, such as the West Cameroon Marketing Board, were merged into or replaced by national bodies.
- Many Anglophones saw the end of federalism as a breach of the agreement of Foumban and a form of assimilation; this feeling is at the origin of the later "Anglophone problem".
- Supporters of the reform argued that a single national budget and a single administration would speed up development in all regions.

**Conclusion.** Ahidjo abolished the federation to build national unity, reduce costs and centralise power; the unitary state strengthened the presidency but ended West Cameroon's autonomy and left a lasting sense of grievance.
